Microscopic Mechanism of High-Temperature Superconductivity Revealed by Ab Initio Studies
on Hole-Doped Multilayer Cuprates 𝐇𝐠𝐁𝐚𝟐​𝐂𝐚𝟐​𝐂𝐮𝟑​𝐎𝟖\mathrm{HgBa_{2}Ca_{2}Cu_{3}O_{8}} under Pressure

Ryui Kaneko Email: ryuikaneko@sophia.ac.jp Affiliation: Physics Division, Sophia University, Chiyoda, Tokyo 102-8554, Japan    Masatoshi Imada Email: imada@g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp Affiliation: Faculty of Engineering, The University of Tokyo, 7-3-1 Hongo, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo 113-8656, Japan Affiliation: Physics Division, Sophia University, Chiyoda, Tokyo 102-8554, Japan
August 22, 2026
Abstract

Triple-layer cuprate superconductor HgBa2​Ca2​Cu3​O8\mathrm{HgBa_{2}Ca_{2}Cu_{3}O_{8}} (Hg1223) keeps the record of the highest superconducting (SC) critical temperature Tc∼134T_{\mathrm{c}}\sim 134 K among all the existing materials at ambient pressure. TcT_{\mathrm{c}} further increases under pressure up to Tc∼160T_{\mathrm{c}}\sim 160 K, thereby holding the key to the realistic and comprehensive understanding of the cuprate superconductors, which is one of the grand challenges in physics. However, the microscopic mechanism of high TcT_{\mathrm{c}} of Hg1223 remains to be elucidated. Here, we perform first-principles calculations of Hg1223 both at ambient and applied pressures by solving ab initio Hamiltonians with an accurate variational solver supplemented by a neural network. The pressure dependence of the calculated dd-wave SC order parameter and estimated TcT_{\mathrm{c}} shows a structure supporting a TcT_{\mathrm{c}} peak around 3030 GPa in quantitative agreement with the reported experimental indications. The origin of the strong SC amplitude of Hg1223 at ambient pressure compared to other cuprates is identified as strong local Coulomb repulsion UU attributed to poorer screening of the Coulomb interaction in multilayer compounds. The origin of the further increase in TcT_{\mathrm{c}} under pressure is ascribed to a unique interplay of three elements, namely increased electron hopping tt, decreased UU, and more importantly, strongly reduced non-local Coulomb repulsion VV with increasing pressure. The origin of Cooper pairing is identified as the emergent local attraction counterintuitively arising from the strong bare local repulsion UU for Hg1223. It explains why Hg1223 shows the highest TcT_{\mathrm{c}} among other cuprates, while the pairing mechanism is common in other cuprates as well. The emergent attraction is interpreted from “attraction from reduced repulsion”, originating from the release of the fluctuating doubly-occupied sites characterized from the “false vacuum” in the Mott insulator to the double-occupation-free dd-wave SC states caused by the carrier doping. This instantaneous and local attraction is in marked contrast with the case of the conventional BCS SC mediated by bosonic glues. The local attraction is consistent with the electron fractionalization supported in experimental analyses. The coexistence of SC and antiferromagnetic (AF) orders is also demonstrated as a characteristic feature of the multilayer system with self-doping in the underdoped region. The quantitative and microscopic understanding of the high TcT_{\mathrm{c}} in Hg1223 provides a new perspective on the origin of the cuprate superconductivity and offers a new route explicitly using this channel of the emergent attraction for future superconductivity research aiming at designing and optimizing SC materials.

I Introduction

Since the discovery of high-temperature superconductors (SCs) in copper oxides (cuprates) in 1986 9, cuprate SCs continue to hold the record of the highest SC critical temperature (TcT_{\mathrm{c}}) at ambient pressure. Although a tremendous amount of research has been conducted with significant advances, understanding the microscopic mechanisms behind materials dependencies of TcT_{\mathrm{c}} and high-TcT_{\mathrm{c}} superconductivity itself continues to be a central challenge in condensed matter physics. Strong electron correlations that characterize the cuprate SCs accompanied by severe competition among intertwined different states and fluctuations require accurate many-body solutions.

Recently, by using state-of-the-art quantum many-body solvers, ab initio low-energy effective Hamiltonians for single-, double-, and infinite-layer cuprates have been solved, which successfully reproduced the rich material-dependence of TcT_{\mathrm{c}} 72. More specifically, based on the effective Hamiltonians for CaCuO2\mathrm{CaCuO_{2}} with an infinite-layer structure, HgBa2​CuO4\mathrm{HgBa_{2}CuO_{4}} (Hg1201), Bi2​Sr2​CuO6\mathrm{Bi_{2}Sr_{2}CuO_{6}} (Bi2201) with a single-layer structure and Bi2​Sr2​CaCu2​O8\mathrm{Bi_{2}Sr_{2}CaCu_{2}O_{8}} (Bi2212) with a double-layer structure by using an accurate variational Monte Carlo (VMC) method 76; 51 combined with a neural network algorithm 60 using only experimental crystal structures as inputs, the material and doping concentration dependencies of the SC order parameter and TcT_{\mathrm{c}} have been quantitatively reproduced. The materials dependence has been understood primarily from the difference in an ab initio Hamiltonian parameter for the dimensionless ratio of the local interaction UU to the nearest-neighbor hopping amplitude |t1||t_{1}|. The severe competition among the SC, antiferromagnetic (AF), and stripe phases is in agreement with the observations in the experiments as well.

However, significantly higher TcT_{\mathrm{c}} was observed in multilayer, especially triple-layer cuprates, while the numerical analysis of the multilayer cuprates on the same level as Ref. [72] is so far missing because of the demanding computational cost ascribed to the large unit cell.

Among all the available materials at ambient pressure, the highest TcT_{\mathrm{c}} was reported at Tc∼134T_{\mathrm{c}}\sim 134 K in a triple-layer cuprate compound HgBa2​Ca2​Cu3​O8\mathrm{HgBa_{2}Ca_{2}Cu_{3}O_{8}} (Hg1223) 65; 71; 20; 16; 84 (see Fig. 1 for the crystal structure). When the pressure is applied, Hg1223 shows a further increased TcT_{\mathrm{c}} forming dome-like pressure dependence and reaches the peak at around 3030 GPa, as high as Tc∼160T_{\mathrm{c}}\sim 160 K, which is the highest record among the cuprates 20; 84. Therefore, without identifying the microscopic origin of such high TcT_{\mathrm{c}} values based on the ab initio parameter-free framework, the mechanism of the cuprate SC would not be ultimately understood.

In this study, we quantitatively elucidate why multilayer cuprates including triple-layer Hg1223 show the substantially higher TcT_{\mathrm{c}} than the single-, double-, and infinite-layer compounds. We also discuss the origin of the observed dome-like pressure dependence of TcT_{\mathrm{c}}, which peaks around 3030 GPa. The materials dependence of the single-, double-, and infinite-layer compounds was captured without paying serious attention to the difference in the off-site interactions because they are similar at ambient pressure 72. Here, by contrast, we show that the pressure-induced reduction of off-site interactions is substantial and plays a major role in enhancing SC. We also clarify that, in the multilayer compounds, the induced self-doping brings about the difference in carrier concentration between the IP and OPs, which allows for the emergence of coexisting SC and AF order as was experimentally observed 57; 46.

Based upon the successful and quantitative reproduction of the materials dependence of the SC for the cuprates including the triple-layer Hg1223, we identify the realistic mechanism of SC: The Cooper pair is induced by the instantaneous and local attraction caused by the reduction of repulsion in the background of strong “vacuum fluctuation”, which is a unique property of the strongly correlated doped Mott insulator. This mechanism is radically different from the conventional BCS SC 8, where the retardation is essential to induce the boson-mediated weak-coupling SC to circumvent the unavoidable electron-electron Coulomb repulsion.

Our calculations are based on the ab initio low-energy effective Hamiltonians of Hg1223 derived in Ref. [55]. The pressure-dependent lattice constants and atomic positions used in deriving these Hamiltonians were obtained from the first-principles structural optimization performed in Ref. [55]. The crystal structure was parameterized by the lattice constants aa and cc and five internal structure parameters, from which the atomic coordinates at each pressure were determined. The relevant hopping parameters were obtained from the matrix elements between maximally localized Wannier orbitals. In the procedure to derive the effective Hamiltonians, Refs. 54; 55 employed a state-of-the-art methodology of constrained GW (cGW) scheme 4; 28; 27, which completely removes the double counting problem known in the constrained RPA 3; 35. In addition, the self-interaction correction (SIC) together with the level renormalization feedback (LRFB) 26 are taken into account, in which the charge distribution among the atomic O2​p2p and Cu3​dx2−y23d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} orbitals, which strongly hybridize to form the antibonding and bonding orbitals, is appropriately treated in a self-consistent fashion. This procedure in total is called cGW-SIC+LRFB scheme. The antibonding orbital constituting the low-energy effective Hamiltonian contains a small portion of other atomic orbitals, such as hybridizing Cu3​d3​z2−r23d_{3z^{2}-r^{2}} and O2​pz2p_{z} orbitals, which contribute to the interlayer hopping. The ground state of the derived effective Hamiltonian for the antibonding orbital on lattices is obtained in this paper by applying the VMC method 76; 51 refined from the seminal work 86; 22; 23; 12. We further enhance the accuracy by combining the VMC method with neural network techniques 13; 60; 61.

This paper is organized as follows: In Sec. II, we briefly describe the ab initio low-energy effective Hamiltonian and the VMC method. In Sec. III, we present the ground states of Hg1223 at ambient pressure obtained by the VMC method. In Sec. IV, we present the pressure dependence of the SC order parameter and TcT_{\mathrm{c}} in Hg1223. In Sec. V, we discuss the effective attraction emergently arising from the strong local repulsion as the origin of Cooper pairing of Hg1223 and compare with the cases of other cuprates with lower TcT_{\mathrm{c}} on the basis of the successful and realistic reproductions of the experimental trend. Section VI is devoted to discussions. Finally, in Sec. VII, we summarize our findings and discuss their consequences. We also provide perspectives for future studies.

II Methods

II.1 Ab initio effective Hamiltonians

We solve the ab initio triple-layer effective Hamiltonian of Hg1223 for the antibonding orbital consisting of strongly hybridized Cu3​dx2−y23d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} and O2​pσ2p_{\sigma} orbitals as derived in Ref. [55], which has the form

ℋ\displaystyle\mathcal{H} =ℋt+ℋU+ℋV+ℋμ\displaystyle=\mathcal{H}_{t}+\mathcal{H}_{U}+\mathcal{H}_{V}+\mathcal{H}_{\mu} (1)

with

ℋt\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{t} =∑I,J,σtI​J​cI,σ†​cJ,σ,\displaystyle=\sum_{I,J,\sigma}t_{IJ}c^{\dagger}_{I,\sigma}c_{J,\sigma}, (2)
ℋU\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{U} =∑IUI​nI,↑​nI,↓,\displaystyle=\sum_{I}U_{I}n_{I,\uparrow}n_{I,\downarrow}, (3)
ℋV\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{V} =12​∑I≠JVI​J​nI​nJ,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{I\neq J}V_{IJ}n_{I}n_{J}, (4)
ℋμ\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\mu} =∑IμI​nI.\displaystyle=\sum_{I}\mu_{I}n_{I}. (5)

Here, II and JJ are multiindices of site and layer, e.g., (i,α)(i,\alpha) and (j,β)(j,\beta), respectively; sites ii and jj correspond to positions 𝒓𝒊=(xi,yi)\bm{r_{i}}=(x_{i},y_{i}) and 𝒓𝒋=(xj,yj)\bm{r_{j}}=(x_{j},y_{j}) on an L×LL\times L square lattice, whereas α\alpha and β\beta indicate the layer, namely, IP or OP. In Fig. 1, here and later, two OPs should be distinguished as OP1 and OP2, where the summations over α\alpha and β\beta run over IP, OP1, and OP2. The operator cI,σ†c^{\dagger}_{I,\sigma} (cI,σc_{I,\sigma}) creates (annihilates) an electron with spin σ\sigma and index II. The operator nI,σ=cI,σ†​cI,σn_{I,\sigma}=c^{\dagger}_{I,\sigma}c_{I,\sigma} counts the number of electrons with spin σ\sigma and index II, and the total number operator is given by nI=nI,↑+nI,↓n_{I}=n_{I,\uparrow}+n_{I,\downarrow}. The system contains one IP and two OPs as shown in Fig. 1, and the total number of sites is Ns=Nl​L2N_{\mathrm{s}}=N_{l}L^{2} with NlN_{l} being the number of layers (Nl=3N_{l}=3 for the triple-layer Hg1223). The hopping parameter is given by tI​Jt_{IJ} and the strengths of the onsite and off-site Coulomb interactions are represented as UIU_{I} and VI​JV_{IJ}, respectively. Both hopping and off-site interaction parameters are functions of the relative coordinate vector 𝒓i−𝒓j\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j} between sites ii and jj because of the translational invariance of the crystal structure. The chemical potential of the IP μI\mu_{I} relative to that of the OP controls the relative carrier densities under the condition of a fixed total number of electrons for a fixed size in the canonical ensemble and is a function of the total number of electrons Ne[=(1−δ)Ns]N_{\mathrm{e}}[=(1-\delta)N_{\mathrm{s}}].

We consider hopping and interaction parameters that extend over long distances and assume that their values are nonzero within the range satisfying r=|𝒓i−𝒓j|≤3​2r=|\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j}|\leq 3\sqrt{2} between sites ii and jj. Here, the distance is counted in the length unit of the nearest Cu-Cu distance both within the x​yxy plane and along the interlayer zz direction. Beyond this range, the parameters are negligibly small. The dominant hopping and interaction parameters employed in the present calculations are summarized in Table 1, for which we employ the values from Ref. [54]. For other parameters, see complete lists in Tables 2, 3 and 4 in Appendix A. They include both intralayer and interlayer parameters. In most cases, the parameters for hopping and interaction are smaller than 1010% of the largest nearest-neighbor hopping and onsite interaction, respectively, when r=|𝒓i−𝒓j|>2r=|\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j}|>2. Although parameters with such small values contribute little to qualitative physical properties, we keep values at longer distances with r>2r>2 up to the 1111th neighbor to perform more realistic simulations of actual systems and for quantitative comparisons with real compounds. The truncated hopping parameters employed in the VMC calculations accurately reproduce the cGW-SIC+LRFB band dispersion near the Fermi level. The resulting Fermi surfaces of the individual bands agree well with those obtained by the full parameter set of the cGW-SIC+LRFB calculations.

The chemical potential difference μ=μOP−μIP\mu=\mu_{\mathrm{OP}}-\mu_{\mathrm{IP}} between the IP and the OP is determined in a way such that μ\mu reproduces the carrier density in each layer obtained by GW calculations. For the details of the determination of μ\mu, see Appendix B. The final hole doping δ\delta dependencies of μ\mu at 00 GPa, 3030 GPa, and 6060 GPa are given by

μ0​GPa\displaystyle\mu_{\mathrm{0\,GPa}} =5.192−9.78​δ,\displaystyle=5.192-9.78\delta, (6)
μ30​GPa\displaystyle\mu_{\mathrm{30\,GPa}} =5.087−11.2​δ,\displaystyle=5.087-11.2\delta, (7)
μ60​GPa\displaystyle\mu_{\mathrm{60\,GPa}} =2.990−6.36​δ,\displaystyle=2.990-6.36\delta, (8)

respectively. At ambient pressure, δIP\delta_{\rm IP} is always smaller than δOP\delta_{\rm OP}. With increasing pressure and doping δ\delta, the chemical potential difference μ\mu becomes smaller, and the carrier densities of the IP and the OP tend to be closer to each other as one can see later in Figs. 2 and 7.

II.2 Numerical methods

We employ an elaborated VMC method, which is available as an open source software 76; 51; 30 for calculating the ground state properties of Hg1223. The variational wave function is given by

|ψ⟩=𝒫G​𝒫J​𝒫dh​|ϕpair⟩,\displaystyle|\psi\rangle=\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{G}}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{J}}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{dh}}|\phi_{\mathrm{pair}}\rangle, (9)

where the Gutzwiller factor 𝒫G\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{G}} 24, the charge Jastrow correlation factor 𝒫J\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{J}} 39; 11, and the doublon-holon correlation factor 𝒫dh\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{dh}} 87 are defined by

𝒫G\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{G}} =exp⁡(∑IgI​nI,↑​nI,↓),\displaystyle=\exp\left(\sum_{I}g_{I}n_{I,\uparrow}n_{I,\downarrow}\right), (10)
𝒫J\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{J}} =exp⁡(∑I<JvI​J​nI​nJ),\displaystyle=\exp\left(\sum_{I<J}v_{IJ}n_{I}n_{J}\right), (11)
𝒫dh\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{dh}} =exp⁡[∑t=1,2∑m=04∑l=d,h∑IγI(t,m,l)​ξI(m,l)],\displaystyle=\exp\left[\sum_{t=1,2}\sum_{m=0}^{4}\sum_{l=\mathrm{d,h}}\sum_{I}\gamma^{(t,m,l)}_{I}\xi^{(m,l)}_{I}\right], (12)

respectively. Here, the doublon is a site occupied by both up- and down-spin electrons and the holon represents an empty site. Variational parameters are gIg_{I}, vI​Jv_{IJ}, and γI(t,m,l)\gamma^{(t,m,l)}_{I}. We assume that gI=g(i,α)g_{I}=g_{(i,\alpha)} does not depend on the position 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i}, but can take different values depending on the layer α\alpha. On the other hand, vI​J=v(i,α)​(j,β)v_{IJ}=v_{(i,\alpha)(j,\beta)} is chosen to be a function of the relative position |𝒓i−𝒓j||\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j}| and can vary for different layer pairs (α,β)(\alpha,\beta). The many-body operator ξI(m,l)\xi^{(m,l)}_{I} is diagonal in the real space representation and takes 11 if a doublon (l=dl=\mathrm{d}) [holon (l=hl=\mathrm{h})] exists at index II and mm holons (doublons) at ttth nearest neighbors surround it; otherwise, ξI(m,l)\xi^{(m,l)}_{I} is 00. The parameter γI(t,m,l)=γ(i,α)(t,m,l)\gamma^{(t,m,l)}_{I}=\gamma^{(t,m,l)}_{(i,\alpha)} does not depend on the position 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i}, but can take different values depending on the layer α\alpha and ttth nearest neighbors. The pair-product wave function 10; 7; 76 is given by

|ϕpair⟩=(∑I,J=1Ns∑σ,σ′fI​Jσ​σ′​cI,σ†​cJ,σ′†)Ne/2​|0⟩,\displaystyle|\phi_{\mathrm{pair}}\rangle=\left(\sum_{I,J=1}^{N_{\mathrm{s}}}\sum_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}f^{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}_{IJ}c^{\dagger}_{I,\sigma}c^{\dagger}_{J,\sigma^{\prime}}\right)^{N_{\mathrm{e}}/2}|0\rangle, (13)

where fI​Jσ​σ′f^{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}_{IJ} are variational parameters and are assumed to have a sublattice structure with translational invariance.

The variational wave function can further be improved by applying additional correlation factors to the aforementioned wave function, and the corresponding energy becomes closer to the exact values by performing a zero-variance extrapolation. We typically consider the wave function with the restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) correlation factor 13; 60; 61, which has the form

|ψRBM⟩=𝒫G​𝒫J​𝒫dh​𝒫RBM​|ϕpair⟩.\displaystyle|\psi_{\mathrm{RBM}}\rangle=\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{G}}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{J}}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{dh}}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{RBM}}|\phi_{\mathrm{pair}}\rangle. (14)

Here, the RBM correlation factor is chosen as

𝒫RBM=exp⁡(∑I,σaI​σ​nI,σ)​∏JNhcosh⁡(bJ+∑I,σWI​J​σ​nI,σ),\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{RBM}}=\exp\left(\sum_{I,\sigma}a_{I\sigma}n_{I,\sigma}\right)\prod_{J}^{N_{\mathrm{h}}}\cosh\left(b_{J}+\sum_{I,\sigma}W_{IJ\sigma}n_{I,\sigma}\right), (15)

with aI​σa_{I\sigma}, bJb_{J}, and WI​J​σW_{IJ\sigma} being variational parameters. Increasing the ratio of the number of hidden parameters NhN_{\mathrm{h}} to the number of sites, namely, αRBM=Nh/Ns\alpha_{\mathrm{RBM}}=N_{\mathrm{h}}/N_{\mathrm{s}}, improves the accuracy of the variational wave function. In practice, we apply the RBM correlation factor on top of the optimized wave function |ψ⟩=𝒫G​𝒫J​𝒫dh​|ϕpair⟩|\psi\rangle=\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{G}}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{J}}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{dh}}|\phi_{\mathrm{pair}}\rangle, although the RBM correlation factor itself can simulate the effects coming from 𝒫G\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{G}} and 𝒫J\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{J}}. Another way of improving the wave function is to consider the Lanczos method 74; 25. We choose the appropriate factors αn\alpha_{n} in the wave function

|ψM⟩=(1+∑n=1Mαn​ℋn)​|ψ⟩\displaystyle|\psi_{M}\rangle=\left(1+\sum_{n=1}^{M}\alpha_{n}\mathcal{H}^{n}\right)|\psi\rangle (16)

so that its energy is minimized. We apply the Lanczos method up to the first step (M=1M=1) 50; 33 in this study because of the high computational cost, which increases exponentially in MM.

We assume antiperiodic-periodic boundary conditions and calculate ground-state candidate states of lattices with Ns=3​L2N_{\mathrm{s}}=3L^{2} sites. The system sizes that we have studied range from L=16L=16 to L=28L=28, where the system contains 23522352 sites at L=28L=28. We first calculate ground-state candidate states and then compare the energy per site E/Ns=⟨H⟩/NsE/N_{\mathrm{s}}=\langle H\rangle/N_{\mathrm{s}} of each state after the variance extrapolation 34; 42; 82 to the zero limit with the help of results obtained after Lanczos and RBM operations if necessary. The variance is evaluated by (δ​E)2=(⟨H2⟩−⟨H⟩2)/⟨H⟩2(\delta E)^{2}=(\langle H^{2}\rangle-\langle H\rangle^{2})/\langle H\rangle^{2} and satisfies δ​E=0\delta E=0 for true eigenstates. We determine the ground state by choosing the one with the lowest energy among the candidate states. Such ground-state candidate states include the SC, metallic, staggered AF, and C4S8 stripe 78; 77 states as well as the coexistence of the SC and AF. See the detailed procedure in Appendix C. Since the Lanczos procedure is generally considered to have negligible effects on analyzed physical quantities such as correlations and order parameters 38; 50; 88; 32, we present order parameters without applying the Lanczos method hereafter.

For important quantities such as SC and AF order parameters, we take the size extrapolation to the thermodynamic limit. In some cases below, however, we only show the results for 24×24×324\times 24\times 3 lattice for Hg1223 with an explicit remark to save the demanding computational time for the size extrapolation, when the size dependence is small.

II.3 Physical quantities

We calculate the spin and charge structure factors to distinguish whether the state exhibits magnetic and charge orders. The spin structure factor in each layer α(=IP,OP)\alpha(=\mathrm{IP},\mathrm{OP}) is defined by

Ssα​(𝒒)=1L2​∑i,j⟨𝑺i,α⋅𝑺j,α⟩​ei​𝒒⋅(𝒓i−𝒓j),\displaystyle S^{\alpha}_{\mathrm{s}}(\bm{q})=\frac{1}{L^{2}}\sum_{i,j}\langle\bm{S}_{i,\alpha}\cdot\bm{S}_{j,\alpha}\rangle e^{i\bm{q}\cdot(\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j})}, (17)

where 𝑺i=(Six,Siy,Siz)=∑τ,τ′ci,τ†​𝝈τ,τ′​ci,τ′/2\bm{S}_{i}=(S^{x}_{i},S^{y}_{i},S^{z}_{i})=\sum_{\tau,\tau^{\prime}}c^{\dagger}_{i,\tau}\bm{\sigma}_{\tau,\tau^{\prime}}c_{i,\tau^{\prime}}/2 is the spin-1/21/2 operator and 𝝈τ,τ′\bm{\sigma}_{\tau,\tau^{\prime}} is the Pauli matrix. Similarly, the charge structure factor in each layer is defined by

Scα​(𝒒)=1L2​∑i,j⟨ni,α​nj,α⟩​ei​𝒒⋅(𝒓i−𝒓j).\displaystyle S^{\alpha}_{\mathrm{c}}(\bm{q})=\frac{1}{L^{2}}\sum_{i,j}\langle n_{i,\alpha}n_{j,\alpha}\rangle e^{i\bm{q}\cdot(\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j})}. (18)

The system exhibits long-range order when Ssα​(𝑸)/L2S^{\alpha}_{\mathrm{s}}(\bm{Q})/L^{2} or Scα​(𝑸)/L2S^{\alpha}_{\mathrm{c}}(\bm{Q})/L^{2} at the Bragg peak 𝑸\bm{Q} is extrapolated to a nonzero value in the thermodynamic limit (L→∞L\to\infty). The order parameter in the thermodynamic limit is evaluated by

ms,cα=limL→∞Ss,cα​(𝒒)L2.\displaystyle m^{\alpha}_{\mathrm{s,c}}=\sqrt{\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{S^{\alpha}_{\mathrm{s,c}}(\bm{q})}{L^{2}}}. (19)

The SC states in the present study are of dd-wave type, and the corresponding SC correlation function in each layer α\alpha is given by

Pdα(𝒓)=1L2∑𝒓i⟨Δdα†(𝒓i)Δdα(𝒓i+𝒓)+H.c.⟩,\displaystyle P^{\alpha}_{d}(\bm{r})=\frac{1}{L^{2}}\sum_{\bm{r}_{i}}\langle{\Delta^{\alpha}_{d}}^{\dagger}(\bm{r}_{i})\Delta^{\alpha}_{d}(\bm{r}_{i}+\bm{r})+\mathrm{H.c.}\rangle, (20)

where Δdα​(𝒓i)\Delta^{\alpha}_{d}(\bm{r}_{i}) is the order parameter with the form

Δdα​(𝒓i)=12​∑𝒓fd​(𝒓)​(c𝒓i,α,↑​c𝒓i+𝒓,α,↓−c𝒓i,α,↓​c𝒓i+𝒓,α,↑).\displaystyle\Delta^{\alpha}_{d}(\bm{r}_{i})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sum_{\bm{r}}f_{d}(\bm{r})(c_{\bm{r}_{i},\alpha,\uparrow}c_{\bm{r}_{i}+\bm{r},\alpha,\downarrow}-c_{\bm{r}_{i},\alpha,\downarrow}c_{\bm{r}_{i}+\bm{r},\alpha,\uparrow}). (21)

The form factor at 𝒓=(x,y)\bm{r}=(x,y) that reflects the dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} symmetry is given by

fd​(𝒓)=δy,0​(δx,1+δx,−1)−δx,0​(δy,1+δy,−1).\displaystyle f_{d}(\bm{r})=\delta_{y,0}(\delta_{x,1}+\delta_{x,-1})-\delta_{x,0}(\delta_{y,1}+\delta_{y,-1}). (22)

For SC states in large systems, the SC correlation function nearly saturates for sufficiently long distances. This long-distance correlation is proportional to the square of the SC order parameter FSCα​(L)F^{\alpha}_{\mathrm{SC}}(L) for a finite system in layer α\alpha. To practically estimate this value, we average the long-distance part of Pdα​(𝒓)P^{\alpha}_{d}(\bm{r}) and evaluate a quantity, which is given by

[FSCα​(L)]2=P¯dα​(L)=1Nfar​∑|𝒓|>2​L/4Pdα​(𝒓).\displaystyle[F^{\alpha}_{\mathrm{SC}}(L)]^{2}=\bar{P}^{\alpha}_{d}(L)=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{far}}}\sum_{|\bm{r}|>\sqrt{2}L/4}P^{\alpha}_{d}(\bm{r}). (23)

Here, position 𝒓=(x,y)\bm{r}=(x,y) runs over all sites within a region (−L/2,L/2]2(-L/2,L/2]^{2} and NfarN_{\mathrm{far}} is the number of lattice points satisfying |𝒓|∈(2​L/4,2​L/2)|\bm{r}|\in(\sqrt{2}L/4,\sqrt{2}L/2). Then, the SC order parameter in the thermodynamic limit FSCα,∞F^{\alpha,\infty}_{\mathrm{SC}} for layer α\alpha is evaluated by

P¯dα,∞\displaystyle\bar{P}^{\alpha,\infty}_{d} =limL→∞P¯dα​(L),\displaystyle=\lim_{L\to\infty}\bar{P}^{\alpha}_{d}(L), (24)
FSCα,∞\displaystyle F^{\alpha,\infty}_{\mathrm{SC}} =limL→∞FSCα​(L)=P¯dα,∞.\displaystyle=\lim_{L\to\infty}F^{\alpha}_{\mathrm{SC}}(L)=\sqrt{\bar{P}^{\alpha,\infty}_{d}}. (25)

The linear 1/L1/L scaling is assumed during the extrapolation 62 because quasiparticle excitations of the dd-wave SC state at nodal points exhibit the Dirac-type linear dispersion.

All the physical quantities including the energy are estimated by the standard Monte Carlo sampling. Error bars for a fixed system size are estimated by the statistical errors of each quantity. In the procedure of size extrapolations, we also estimate the error bars coming from the extrapolation.

III Results at Ambient Pressure

In this section, we show the solutions for the ground state of the effective Hamiltonian for Hg1223 at ambient pressure and discuss SC properties competing with AF and stripe states. A characteristic feature of the multilayer compounds, not present in the single-, double-, and infinite-layer compounds, is self-doping, in which the carrier concentration is self-optimized and varies among layers. Figure 2 shows how the inner- and outer-layer hole densities, δIP\delta_{\rm IP} and δOP\delta_{\rm OP}, respectively, evolve as a function of averaged hole density per layer δ=(δIP+2​δOP)/3\delta=(\delta_{\rm IP}+2\delta_{\rm OP})/3 for the ab initio Hamiltonian of Hg1223 at ambient pressure. From Eq. (6), the IP always has a lower chemical potential of electrons (higher chemical potential of holes) in the realistic carrier density region, so that the IP has a lower hole density. This is consistent with the experimental indications of the multilayer compounds 57; 46.

III.1 Doping concentration dependence of SC order

We show the hole density (δ\delta) dependence of the SC order parameter FSCF_{\rm SC} in the thermodynamic limit at the IP and OP (two OPs show the same behavior) in Fig. 3. Hereafter, for FSC∞F_{\rm SC}^{\infty} obtained after the extrapolation to the thermodynamic limit, we drop ∞\infty as FSCF_{\rm SC}. (The procedure of obtaining FSCF_{\rm SC} from the extrapolation of the SC correlation PdP_{d} to the thermodynamic limit is described in Appendices D and E.) The dominance of the dd-wave SC order demonstrates the consistency with the experimental indications. The optimum value of FSC∼0.14F_{\rm SC}\sim 0.14 at δ=0.14\delta=0.14–0.160.16 is found in the IP and exceeds the maximum value ∼0.13\sim 0.13 of the single-, double-, and infinite-layer compounds reported for Bi2212 72. The origin of the highest optimum FSCF_{\rm SC} among the cuprates studied here and in Ref. [72] is mainly attributed to the highest value of U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| due to the poor screening. The optimum hole density is roughly consistent with Cu valence measurement 19; 84 and NMR data 45 by considering its temperature dependence.

The IP and OP exhibit a similar doping dependence of the SC dome structure. In fact, although the Hamiltonian parameters are similar between the IP and OP at ambient pressure except for the chemical potential, FSCF_{\rm SC} shows the maximum at δIP=0.06\delta_{\rm IP}=0.06 for the IP while at δOP=0.12\delta_{\rm OP}=0.12 for the OP if we plot as a function of the hole density in each layer as is seen in Fig. 4. This shift between the IP and OP cannot be explained if the IP and OP are independent. On the other hand, the shift can be caused by the synchronization between the IP and OP as one sees as a function of the averaged density δ\delta in Fig. 3 suggesting a substantial interlayer proximity effect, which may also enhance the amplitude of FSCF_{\rm SC} at the IP relative to the OP because the IP is sandwiched by the two OPs. To assess the role of parameter inhomogeneity at 00 GPa, we also set the OP parameters equal to the IP parameters and find nearly unchanged doping dependence of the SC order parameters, indicating that the inhomogeneity has little effect on them. We emphasize that this interlayer proximity effect occurs near ambient pressure, where the Hamiltonian parameters for the IP and OP do not differ significantly. Under pressure, however, the parameter difference between the two layers becomes more pronounced. Indeed, at 6060 GPa, the off-site Coulomb interactions in the IP become substantially stronger than those in the OP (see Table 1); therefore, the interlayer proximity effect is not strong enough to make the perfect synchronization.

III.2 Coexistence of AF and SC

The carrier density in the IP is much closer to the half filling than that in the OP, which tends to stabilize AF order in the IP, while the OP stabilizes SC order. Therefore, if the interlayer coupling is switched off by keeping the self-doped hole density, one would expect the segregation and independent survival of the SC order in the OP and the AF order in the IP in an appropriate range of the averaged hole density, because the microscopic coexistence is not seen in the numerical result of the single-, double-, and infinite-layer cuprates 72. However, this segregation is not a microscopic coexistence, but an interlayer phase separation. If a small but nonzero tunneling is introduced between the segregated IP and OP, as in the realistic situation of the multilayer cuprates, the proximity may lead to the coexistence in both planes. Here, we discuss such a possibility of the microscopic and homogeneous coexistence of AF and SC orders at ambient pressure.

To see a typical example, we focus on the case of 88% doping on average. When we use the ab initio Hamiltonian for Hg1223 at ambient pressure, the IP becomes nearly half-filled by the self-doping and exhibits the AF order. However, in the underdoped region, the GW calculation tends to be less reliable due to the strong correlation effect of the precursor to the Mott insulator in the real compounds ignored in the GW calculation, which implies that the approach to the Mott insulator in the IP will be slower in reality in accordance with the experimental indications. To mimic this effect, we study the effect of μ\mu reduced from the GW adjusted value, μ=4.41\mu=4.41 to μ=3.2\mu=3.2, which makes the difference in δIP\delta_{\rm IP} and δOP\delta_{\rm OP} smaller to δIP=0.07\delta_{\rm IP}=0.07 and δOP=0.085\delta_{\rm OP}=0.085 instead of δIP=0\delta_{\rm IP}=0 and δOP=0.12\delta_{\rm OP}=0.12 for μ=4.41\mu=4.41. (For the detailed analyses regarding the dependence on the chemical potential difference between the IP and OPs, please see Appendix F.)

Figure 5 shows the SC and AF correlations in the OP and IP for a 24×2424\times 24 lattice. The size extrapolation to the thermodynamic limit in Fig. 6 indeed supports the coexistence. (See also Fig. 24. The coexisting state has the lowest energy below the uniform SC and uniform AF states. We have not studied the comparison with possible long-period stripe states, which is left for future studies.) The result supports the coexistence at the inner layer in a certain range of parameters by the mechanism of proximity from the robust SC order in the outer layer that lowers the energy from a uniform non-SC AF state. The coexistence of the AF and SC in multilayer cuprates is overall consistent with experiments 57; 46; 31.

IV Results under Pressure

In this section, we show the solutions for the ground state under pressure, especially the pressure dependence of the SC order parameter and TcT_{\mathrm{c}}.

IV.1 Pressure dependence of SC order

Figure 7 illustrates the δ\delta dependence of nIP=1−δIPn_{\rm IP}=1-\delta_{\rm IP} and nOP=1−δOPn_{\rm OP}=1-\delta_{\rm OP} while Fig. 8 shows the SC order parameter in the thermodynamic limit, FSCF_{\rm SC} in the IP and OP at 3030 and 6060 GPa, which confirms the dominance of the SC order for δ>0.12\delta>0.12 even under pressure. For detailed data for finite sizes and their size extrapolations, see Appendices D and E. Both at 3030 GPa and 6060 GPa, FSCF_{\rm SC} is comparable between the IP and OP while in most cases, the IP shows slightly larger FSCF_{\rm SC}. In Fig. 9, we plot FSCF_{\rm SC} for all the pressures at the hole density δ=0.16\delta=0.16, which is the optimal value at ambient pressure. Since FSCF_{\rm SC} is always larger for the IP than for the OP at δ=0.16\delta=0.16, we plot only the values for the IP. The SC order parameter FSCF_{\mathrm{SC}} (black circles) remains nearly constant from 00 GPa to 3030 GPa and decreases from 3030 GPa to 6060 GPa. We analyze the origin of this trend below. In the inset of Fig. 9, the pressure dependence of the Hamiltonian parameters |t1||t_{1}|, U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| and V1/|t1|V_{1}/|t_{1}| at the IP are plotted by taking the data from Tables 2, 3 and 4. From 00 to 6060 GPa, |t1||t_{1}| increases, while U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| and V1/|t1|V_{1}/|t_{1}| decrease significantly. In particular, V1/|t1|V_{1}/|t_{1}| decreases to less than a half.

We plot FSCF_{\rm SC} at δ=0.16\delta=0.16 in Fig. 10 for four choices of pressures of Hg1223 at the corresponding values of U/|t1|U/|t_{1}|. We also plot FSCF_{\rm SC} for the infinite-, single-, and double-layer compounds, CaCuO2, Hg1201, Bi2201, and Bi2212 at the optimal doping and ambient pressure taken from Ref. [72] together. The data for Hg1223 under pressure clearly deviate from the universal trend for the single-, double-, and infinite-layer compounds at ambient pressure grouped by the shaded belt. This implies that FSCF_{\rm SC} is not solely determined by U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| under pressure. In fact, although the off-site Coulomb interaction is similar among various cuprates at ambient pressure (for instance, the nearest-neighbor Coulomb interaction V1∼1V_{1}\sim 1 eV, see Table 5), it is decreased substantially under pressure (for instance, V1∼0.88V_{1}\sim 0.88 eV and 0.680.68 eV at 3030 GPa and 6060 GPa, respectively) (see Appendix A for details). This reduction is along the same line as the reduction of UU under pressure (UU for Hg1223 is ∼4.52\sim 4.52, 4.364.36, and 4.184.18 eV at 00, 3030, and 6060 GPa, respectively), which is ascribed to the increased screening from the block layers and apical oxygens caused by the shrunk lattice constant under pressure. It shares a common feature observed before in quasi 2D systems 58, where the reduction of Coulomb interaction caused by the off-plane screening is similar irrespective of the mutual distance (namely, regardless of whether U,V1,V2,…U,V_{1},V_{2},...) (and hence the reduction is relatively more significant for larger mutual distance).

The large enhancement of FSCF_{\mathrm{SC}} by the reduction of the off-site interaction was actually pointed out in Ref. [72], and the present result is consistent with it. The gradual pressure dependence of FSCF_{\rm SC} for Hg1223 instead of the steeper reduction in the general trend at ambient pressure is now understood by the interplay of reduced UU and V1V_{1} (and reduced ViV_{i} with i>2i>2 as well), where the reduction of FSCF_{\rm SC} by reduced U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| is partially compensated by a large reduction of the off-site interactions.

To corroborate our understanding of the effect of the reduced off-site interaction under pressure, we calculated for a hypothetical system of modified single-layer Hg1201, where we reduced only the off-site interactions (Vi,i≥1V_{i},i\geq 1) from the ab initio values of Hg1201 with the factor ξ=0.686\xi=0.686 as ξ​Vi\xi V_{i} at nearly 1515% doping concentration (δ=0.146\delta=0.146). Here, this factor ξ\xi mimics Vi/|t1|V_{i}/|t_{1}| for pressurized Hg1223 that has U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| corresponding to Hg1201. The result is plotted as a red open square in Fig. 10, which indeed fits the trend of Hg1223 under pressure. In the multilayer systems, there seems to be an additional cooperative effect from the OP and IP through the proximity to further enhance the SC.

This suggests the importance of controlling the off-site interaction in material design, as is already pointed out in hypothetical parameter search 72. The proposal in Ref. [72] indeed becomes a reality here as the pressure effect, which works to reduce the effective interaction in the relative ratio to the values for ambient pressure more efficiently for the off-site part than for the onsite one, which helps enhance the superconductivity in Hg1223. If UU could be retained under pressure simultaneously with reduced off-site interaction, FSCF_{\rm SC} could be much more enhanced as we will discuss below.

IV.2 Pressure dependence of TcT_{\mathrm{c}}

It was proposed that TcT_{\mathrm{c}} at the optimum hole density can be estimated by using the ab initio result in the scaling form

Tc∼0.16​|t1|​FSC\displaystyle T_{\mathrm{c}}\sim 0.16|t_{1}|F_{\rm SC} (26)

for the single-, double-, and infinite-layer compounds at ambient pressure 72. Since FSCF_{\rm SC} of Hg1223 under pressure does not follow the common trend of cuprates at ambient pressure and the triple-layer structure contains non-equivalent IP and OP, it is highly nontrivial whether this scaling form is also valid in the triple-layer Hg1223 under pressure.

To test the validity, in Fig. 11, we plot the pressure dependence of TcT_{\mathrm{c}} estimated by using Eq. (26) together with t1t_{1} and the calculated FSCF_{\rm SC} at the IP responsible for the higher TcT_{\mathrm{c}} and compare it with the experimental TcT_{\mathrm{c}} reported in Refs. [20], [84], and [40]. The experimental and numerical values of TcT_{\mathrm{c}} agree fairly well at 00 and 3030 GPa and they are maximized around 3030 GPa, which supports the validity of the scaling form (26) under pressure for the triple-layer compound despite the large deviation of FSCF_{\rm SC} from the trend in the single-, double-, and infinite-layer compounds at ambient pressure.

Note that beyond 3030 GPa, TcT_{\mathrm{c}} in the experimental report is largely uncertain, because only one report exists 20, where only the onset temperature for the superconductivity is available, and the zero resistivity was not reached at any temperature, implying the inhomogeneity in samples or possible non-uniformity of hydrostatic pressure.

The origin of the TcT_{\mathrm{c}} peak structure in Hg1223 under pressure is now understood from the scaling form (26): With increasing pressure, the SC order parameter FSCF_{\rm SC} is nearly constant up to 3030 GPa and then decreases above 3030 GPa, whereas the nearest-neighbor hopping parameter |t1||t_{1}| monotonically increases. To keep the plateau of FSCF_{\rm SC}, the reduction of off-site Coulomb repulsion plays an important role. Then the pressure dependence of TcT_{\mathrm{c}} exhibits a maximum in the intermediate pressure region near 3030 GPa, as shown in Fig. 11, because of the interplay between FSCF_{\rm SC} and |t1||t_{1}|.

In Fig. 12, we show the comparison between the experimental TcT_{\mathrm{c}} and the present estimates for CaCuO2, Hg1201, Bi2201, Bi2212 and Hg1223 at ambient pressure as well as Hg1223 under pressure. The ab initio estimates essentially reproduce all the experimental indications. In particular, it captures the experimental trend of the higher TcT_{\mathrm{c}} of Hg1223 in comparison to others.

V Effective attraction

To understand the mechanism of superconductivity, it is crucially important to uncover the origin of the effective attraction that causes the Cooper pairing. In this section, we report a detailed analysis obtained from the ab initio calculations, which should be relevant to both Hg1223 and other cuprate compounds.

In general, effective static interaction of particles can be estimated from the energy required to add a particle to the system. Namely, the effective interaction energy between the added particle and the particles already existing in the system is measured by the shift of the chemical potential from an NN-particle system μ⁡(N)\mu(N) to that of an N+1N+1-particle system μ⁡(N+1)\mu(N+1), in other words, μ⁡(N+1)−μ⁡(N)∼∂μ/∂n\mu(N+1)-\mu(N)\sim\partial\mu/\partial n. Since μ=∂E∂n\mu=\frac{\partial E}{\partial n} with nn and EE being the particle density and the energy density, respectively, the effective interaction is given by ∂2E∂n2\frac{\partial^{2}E}{\partial n^{2}}. Partial interaction energy can also be defined by decomposing the total energy density EE into the sum of partial energies by following the proposal in Ref. [72]. Here, by decomposing Eq. (1) into Eqs. (2)-(5), we focus on the local interaction, ∂2EU∂δ2\frac{\partial^{2}E_{U}}{\partial\delta^{2}}, where EU=⟨ℋU⟩E_{U}=\langle{\mathcal{H}}_{U}\rangle denotes the ground state average of the local interaction.

To estimate the effective interaction at δ=δm\delta=\delta_{m} practically, we fit the onsite Coulomb energy EU​(δ)E_{U}(\delta) by the quadratic function

EU​(δ)=c0+c1​(δ−δm)+c2​(δ−δm)2,\displaystyle E_{U}(\delta)=c_{0}+c_{1}(\delta-\delta_{m})+c_{2}(\delta-\delta_{m})^{2}, (27)

where c0c_{0}, c1c_{1}, and c2c_{2} are the fitting parameters. The coefficient c2c_{2} is the effective interaction, and we rewrite it in terms of the effective attraction g≡−c2g\equiv-c_{2} hereafter. We typically consider EUE_{U} at five discrete and adjacent hole densities, say, δ1<δ2<δ3<δ4<δ5\delta_{1}<\delta_{2}<\delta_{3}<\delta_{4}<\delta_{5} and assign the quadratic fitting parameter c2c_{2} around δm=δ3\delta_{m}=\delta_{3} as the interaction strength.

We show U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| dependence of the effective attraction gg and the SC order parameter FSCF_{\rm SC} for a number of choices of δ\delta in Fig. 13 and 14, respectively, for Hg1223 at 00, 3030 and 6060 GPa. In this analysis, EUE_{U} is further decomposed into the IP and OP contributions, and we choose the curvature of either the IP or OP that shows the stronger SC order parameter. As references, we also show gg and FSCF_{\rm SC} calculated for hypothetical Hamiltonians modified from that of the hole-doped CaCuO2 only by changing the UU value by hand from the ab initio value U=4.22U=4.22 eV (U/|t1|=8.1U/|t_{1}|=8.1).

In the case of CaCuO2 and its derivatives, the effective attraction gg shown in Fig. 13 is enhanced in underdoped regions and is maximized at the interaction U/|t1|∼9U/|t_{1}|\sim 9 in the realistic range 8≤U/|t1|≤128\leq U/|t_{1}|\leq 12. The attraction is gradually reduced with increasing doping. The attraction gg for the triple-layer cuprate, Hg1223, in overall trend, agrees well with that of CaCuO2 at the corresponding values of U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| and δ\delta. This means that the effective attraction generated by the onsite repulsive Coulomb interaction emerges in the same way in all the single-, double-, triple-, and infinite-layer cuprates.

The SC order parameter FSCF_{\rm SC} is shown in Fig. 14 for the Hamiltonians for CaCuO2, and its derivatives, which also shows the maxima at the interaction U/|t1|∼9U/|t_{1}|\sim 9, just as in the case of gg. Furthermore, the peak structure is asymmetric around the peak in both gg and FSCF_{\rm SC}: The tail is steeper for the weak coupling side U/|t1|<9U/|t_{1}|<9, whereas it is broader for the strong-coupling side U/|t1|>9U/|t_{1}|>9. The SC order parameter of the triple-layer cuprate, Hg1223, follows the trend of CaCuO2, although FSCF_{\rm SC} is higher at higher pressure thanks to the reduced off-site Coulomb interaction in Hg1223 as is discussed in Sec. IV.1. The overall similar behavior between gg and FSCF_{\rm SC} in U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| and δ\delta dependencies with a prominent peak around U/|t1|∼9U/|t_{1}|\sim 9 and asymmetric U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| dependence around the peak strongly supports that the local attraction gg is indeed the origin of the SC order.

However, there exist two important different trends between gg and FSCF_{\rm SC}. 1) One is the hole density dependence: gg increases strongly with decreasing hole density, while FSCF_{\rm SC} shows much smaller δ\delta dependence. 2) The other is that FSCF_{\rm SC} shows a clear deviation for Hg1223 under pressure from the trend of modified CaCuO2, namely, substantially enhanced FSCF_{\rm SC} for Hg1223 at 3030 and 6060 GPa than the modified CaCuO2 is observed, as is already ascribed to the effect of off-site interaction in Sec. IV.1. On the other hand, gg does not show such an enhancement for Hg1223 under pressure. These discrepancies give us insights into the nature of superconductivity.

On point 1), we note that the attractive interaction induces the SC order, but they are not the same. In fact, it is known experimentally that the SC gap monotonically increases with decreasing hole concentration δ\delta even in the underdoped region while TcT_{\mathrm{c}} has a dome structure and decreases to zero toward the Mott insulator 2. This detachment has the same origin as the difference between gg and FSCF_{\rm SC}. Namely, at least in the underdoped region, FSCF_{\rm SC} must decrease with the carrier density 68 and must vanish at the transition to the insulator, while gg may remain nonzero. Therefore, FSCF_{\rm SC} is expected to be better represented by gg multiplied by δ\delta at least in the underdoped region.

Based on this observation, we plot (g+A)​δ(g+A)\delta in Fig. 15, where AA is 2. The offset AA is considered because even for noninteracting fermions, where the local interaction vanishes as well, c2=−gc_{2}=-g must be positive because of the Pauli exclusion principle, and the origin of the local interaction should be located at a negative gg, which makes the effective attraction g+Ag+A with the positive offset AA. The value of AA can be inferred from the value of c2c_{2} at small UU. Figure 15 shows a better correlation with FSCF_{\rm SC} than Fig. 13 on the point that the large enhancement in the undoped region is suppressed around the relevant region U/|t1|∼8U/|t_{1}|\sim 8-10.

Let us discuss the point 2). We have addressed that FSCF_{\rm SC} is dominantly determined by gg at ambient pressure. However, it is likely that off-site effective interactions play a certain role, which may show up as the off-site interaction dependence of AA, namely, AA is similar at ambient pressure because the off-site interactions are similar (for instance V1∼1V_{1}\sim 1 eV throughout the cuprates), while AA should increase substantially under pressure due to reduced off-site interaction consistently with the finding in Sec. IV.1. This well resolves the point 2). It implies that

FSC∼18​g∗|t1|​δF_{\rm SC}\sim\frac{1}{8}\frac{g^{*}}{|t_{1}|}\delta (28)

is roughly satisfied in the realistic region, where the effective total attraction g∗=g+Ag^{*}=g+A, after including the effect of off-site interaction in AA, can generally be expressed by the dimensionless scaling function GG as g∗=|t1|​G​(t2|t1|,t3|t1|,…,U|t1|,V1|t1|,…)g^{*}=|t_{1}|G(\frac{t_{2}}{|t_{1}|},\frac{t_{3}}{|t_{1}|},\dots,\frac{U}{|t_{1}|},\frac{V_{1}}{|t_{1}|},\dots). The calculated results indicate that GG most dominantly depends on U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| and secondarily on V1/|t1|V_{1}/|t_{1}| as FSCF_{\rm SC}.

The finding of the close correlation between FSCF_{\rm SC} and the local and instantaneous emergent attraction gg looks to support a SC mechanism entirely different from the conventional one mediated by some bosonic glue, such as the dynamical spin or charge fluctuation scenarios. In fact, it introduces an unexplored perspective as we will discuss below. However, we also make a remark on the relation to the spin-fluctuation scenario. The spin fluctuation can be measured by the dynamical spin structure factor

Ss​(𝒒,ω)=1L2​∫d​t​∑i,j⟨𝑺i​(t=0)⋅𝑺j​(t)⟩​ei​𝒒⋅(𝒓i−𝒓j)+i​ω​t,\displaystyle S_{\mathrm{s}}(\bm{q},\omega)=\frac{1}{L^{2}}\int dt\sum_{i,j}\langle\bm{S}_{i}(t=0)\cdot\bm{S}_{j}(t)\rangle e^{i\bm{q}\cdot(\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j})+i\omega t}, (29)

while the local Coulomb energy EUE_{U} can be rewritten by using the local moment ⟨m2⟩=⟨S2⟩=34​⟨(ni,↑−ni,↓)2⟩=34​(⟨ni⟩−2​⟨ni,↑​ni,↓⟩)\langle m^{2}\rangle=\langle S^{2}\rangle=\frac{3}{4}\langle(n_{i,\uparrow}-n_{i,\downarrow})^{2}\rangle=\frac{3}{4}(\langle n_{i}\rangle-2\langle n_{i,\uparrow}n_{i,\downarrow}\rangle) as

EU=U⁡[Ne2​Ns−23​∫d​ω​𝑑𝒒​Ss​(𝒒,ω)].\displaystyle E_{U}=U\left[\frac{N_{\rm e}}{2N_{\rm s}}-\frac{2}{3}\int d\omega d\bm{q}S_{\mathrm{s}}(\bm{q},\omega)\right]. (30)

Therefore, the local attraction measures the energy-momentum integrated amplitude of the dynamical spin correlation as

g=2​U3​∂2∂δ2​∫d​ω​𝑑𝒒​Ss​(𝒒,ω).\displaystyle g=\frac{2U}{3}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\delta^{2}}\int d\omega d\bm{q}S_{\mathrm{s}}(\bm{q},\omega). (31)

Since Ss​(𝒒,ω)S_{\mathrm{s}}(\bm{q},\omega) is extended not only to the so-called spin fluctuation region 𝒒∼(π,π)\bm{q}\sim(\pi,\pi) and paramagnon energy range or superexchange range ω<J∼4​t12/U\omega<J\sim 4t_{1}^{2}/U but also to a much wider range in doped Mott insulators, it makes a very broad structure of Ss​(𝒒,ω)S_{\mathrm{s}}(\bm{q},\omega). In the weak coupling SC materials, the attraction is limited to the characteristic energy range of glue around the Fermi surface, such as the Debye frequency for phonon-mediated SC, while in the present case, a much wider range of energy comparable even to the Mott gap is involved, where the picture of instantaneous attraction becomes relevant. In strongly correlated systems, it is often not appropriate to employ the analysis localized in momentum-energy space; rather, it is better to start from a spatially and temporally local picture. See Appendix G for further analyses of attraction.

VI Discussion

Here, we discuss why the local emergent attraction arises counterintuitively from the originally strong repulsion term EUE_{U}. The strong Coulomb repulsion suppresses the double occupation of electrons and induces the AF Mott insulating state at half filling. The Mott insulator is regarded as the “vacuum” of the charge carrier protected by the charge gap. Nevertheless, the averaged double occupation D=⟨ni↑​ni↓⟩D=\langle n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}\rangle and the corresponding exciton density (the density of the bound doublon and holon) do not vanish unless UU becomes infinite. Keeping in mind this common property of the Mott insulator, and the fact that the emergent attraction generated by the UU term shows similar behavior among all the cuprates including Hg1223, we analyze an example of CaCuO2 to elucidate the origin of the attraction.

We show in Fig. 16 U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| dependence of EUE_{U} in the case of the modified CaCuO2 Hamiltonians. There exist peaks around U/|t1|∼6.5U/|t_{1}|\sim 6.5 with inflection points around U/|t1|∼8U/|t_{1}|\sim 8-99. Even the simple Hubbard model in the metastable dd-wave SC state shows a qualitatively common trend, as is shown in Fig. 26 in Appendix G. The nonzero EUE_{U} in the limit δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0 may be interpreted as the “vacuum polarization” energy, and the Mott insulator at δ=0\delta=0 is regarded as the “false vacuum” particularly in the intermediate U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| because of large quantum fluctuations.

This vacuum-polarization structure is in contrast to the band insulator, where the charge density does not fluctuate from zero or two per site, depending on the unoccupied or occupied band, respectively, and the exciton density is strictly zero in the ground state. In the present case of the Mott insulator, the vacuum polarization (quantum fluctuation) generates a nonzero density of doublon-holon pair (exciton) causing high zero-point energy of EUE_{U}.

The introduction of charge carriers induces the collapse of the Mott insulator (collapse of the gap) accompanied by the release of the zero-point energy by rapidly reduced doublon-holon pair density and hence EUE_{U} as one sees in Fig. 16 most prominently in the intermediate U/|t1|∼5U/|t_{1}|\sim 5-9. This nonlinear reduction of the local energy from the “false vacuum” with negative curvature results in the relative local attraction playing the role of the origin of the Cooper pairing. This mechanism may be called “attraction by reduced repulsion”. In the cuprates, EUE_{U} peaks around U/|t1|∼6.5U/|t_{1}|\sim 6.5, and the inflection point around U/|t1|∼8U/|t_{1}|\sim 8-9 in the Mott insulator is indeed the parameter region of the largest attraction g+Ag+A and the strongest SC order parameter FSCF_{\rm SC} as is illustrated in Figs. 15 and 14. The universality of this trend is discussed in Appendix G.

The dd-wave SC state changes the sign of the order parameter across the nodal line in the Brillouin zone and prohibits the double occupation of electrons on the same site by symmetry. Therefore, it has a large energy gain if the order develops by reducing EUE_{U}, which largely contributes to stabilizing the dd-wave SC state against AF, stripe, and Fermi liquid metal, because these competing states allow the double occupation. By the energy gain, the SC order grows, which is accelerated by the nonlinear reduction of EUE_{U} with the negative curvature of δ\delta dependence generating emergent attraction synergetically in a self-consistent fashion.

A complementary view for the conversion from the repulsion to the attraction in the nodal dd-wave SC state is known by considering the scattering process arising from the UU term containing U​ck↑†​c−k↓†​c−q↓​cq↑Uc^{\dagger}_{k\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{-k\downarrow}c_{-q\downarrow}c_{q\uparrow} with k∼(π,0)k\sim(\pi,0) and q∼(0,π)q\sim(0,\pi) 70. This generates the momentum transfer (π,π)(\pi,\pi), which is enhanced if the AF fluctuation is large, while in the mean-field decoupling ⟨ck↑†​c−k↓†⟩​⟨c−q↓​cq↑⟩\langle c^{\dagger}_{k\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{-k\downarrow}\rangle\langle c_{-q\downarrow}c_{q\uparrow}\rangle, the dd-wave phase change between (π,0)(\pi,0) and (0,π)(0,\pi) converts the repulsion U>0U>0 into attraction.

The tight connection between the emergence of attraction and the role of dd-wave SC is clearly seen in Fig. 17, which shows a sharp contrast of the δ\delta dependence of EUE_{U} between the normal metal and the SC state for CaCuO2. Only the dd-wave SC state shows the negative curvature and thus the emergent attraction. Note that the normal metal compared here is different from the metal at temperatures above TcT_{\mathrm{c}} with the pseudogap.

As shown in Figs. 11 and 12, the theoretically estimated TcT_{\mathrm{c}} exhibits a peak at ∼30\sim 30 GPa upon increasing pressure behaving consistently with the experimental TcT_{\mathrm{c}}. On the other hand, the estimated TcT_{\mathrm{c}} is slightly lower for stronger pressure. One of the possible origins is the inhomogeneity of applied pressure in the experiments, which unsettles the definition of the experimental TcT_{\mathrm{c}}: For stronger pressure, the experimentally observed onset temperatures (Tc,onsetT_{\mathrm{c,onset}}) available so far are much higher than the other Tc,midT_{\mathrm{c,mid}} determined by the inflection point of the temperature derivative of the resistivity.

Among a huge number of studies, let us pick up some work, which pays attention to the relation between TcT_{\mathrm{c}} and materials parameters from general viewpoints on the cuprates, which might have relations to the present work. The importance of the apical oxygen position to control TcT_{\mathrm{c}} was empirically pointed out in the cuprates in general in 63. Also empirically, parameters of the crystal structure controlling TcT_{\mathrm{c}} were discussed 44; 1. Several experimental studies on the cuprates reported the relation between TcT_{\mathrm{c}} and the character of dopant atoms and disorder 5; 29. The optimum value for the highest TcT_{\mathrm{c}} was discussed in the U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| dependence 59; 43. Features of the crystal structure to optimize the SC were discussed with the help of machine learning 53. Further studies on the relation between the above work and the present results await future analyses.

On the other hand, many studies pointed out relations between TcT_{\mathrm{c}} and other physical quantities such as SC energy gaps and AF spin-fluctuation energies. For instance, the Uemura plot focused on the proportionality of TcT_{\mathrm{c}} and the SC carrier density measured by the μ\muSR penetration depth in more comprehensive studies on the materials, not only on the cuprates 79. This essentially shares the common viewpoint with Eq. (26). It was pointed out that the scaling Tc∝FSCT_{\mathrm{c}}\propto F_{\rm SC} can be understood from the scaling of the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition temperature in a weakly interacting 2D Bose gas, TBKT∝nbT_{\rm BKT}\propto n_{b} 64 by interpreting the superfluid density FSCF_{\rm SC} as the boson density nbn_{b} in the BEC picture. However, it does not tell us how FSCF_{\rm SC} is determined theoretically, which the present work has elucidated for the cuprates, especially with the pressure dependence of Hg1223 by the ab initio studies. In fact, Eq. (28) unveils the origin of the SC caused by the instantaneous, local, and emergent attraction. We note that FSCF_{\rm SC} is quantitatively consistent with the value reported in Ref. [80] as discussed in Ref. [72].

There exist several studies on the multilayer cuprates. Differentiation in roles of the IP and OP was theoretically emphasized in realizing the high TcT_{\mathrm{c}} of Hg1223 49; 48. While the difference in the hole density they presumed is qualitatively similar to the present result, and the interlayer differentiation plays a role through the proximity, the main origin of the higher TcT_{\mathrm{c}} is found to be ascribed to high U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| in the present work with quantitative agreement with the experiments.

A recent study 6 on Hg1223 at ambient pressure, based on the atomic orbital basis combined with the dynamical mean-field framework similarly to the choice of Ref. [15], instead of the bonding-antibonding basis of strongly hybridized Cu3​dx2−y23d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} and O2​pσ2p_{\sigma} orbitals employed in the present work, proposed a different view. Ref. [6] obtained similar optimum SC order parameter at ambient pressure between Hg1201 and Hg1223 although the experimental optimum TcT_{\mathrm{c}} is substantially different (∼98\sim 98 K for Hg1201 and ∼134\sim 134 K for Hg1223), while the present work correctly captures this experimental trend of difference.

The advantage of the present work solving the lattice Hamiltonian is that this approach is able to treat the spatial and temporal quantum fluctuations on equal footing, which also allows treating the severe competitions of different orders and fluctuations as well beyond mean-field approximations. From the present ab initio work, detailed microscopic origins of dependencies on materials, hole density, and pressure have been elucidated by one-to-one correspondence to the ab initio parameters of the effective Hamiltonians, which makes the microscopic origins and mechanisms of the materials dependence clear and intuitively transparent. It also helps in understanding the physical origin of the empirical relations suggested in the literature discussed in the last paragraphs.

We now briefly mention guiding principles for realizing higher TcT_{\mathrm{c}} than the available materials along the line of the mechanism of the cuprate SC. Since the TcT_{\mathrm{c}} formula (Eq. (26)) widely holds, the strategy to be employed is to design 1) a wider bandwidth (consequently larger |t1||t_{1}|) and 2) larger FSCF_{\rm SC} simultaneously. We learned in the present study that FSCF_{\rm SC} becomes optimized at 2-a) U/|t1|∼9U/|t_{1}|\sim 9 while 2-b) smaller V1/|t1|V_{1}/|t_{1}| enhances FSCF_{\rm SC}. In real materials, it is not easy to satisfy 1), 2-a) and 2-b) simultaneously, because, for instance, the hydrostatic pressure makes the bandwidth wider while U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| and V1/|t1|V_{1}/|t_{1}| (and also V2/|t1|,V3/|t1|​…V_{2}/|t_{1}|,V_{3}/|t_{1}|...) smaller, which have opposite effects on FSCF_{\rm SC}. A possible direction is to search for the materials that have relatively small V1/U,V2/U,…V_{1}/U,V_{2}/U,... within the range of stable SC against the stripe (note that very small ViV_{i} generally is subject to making the stripe state more stable) by keeping U/|t1|∼9U/|t_{1}|\sim 9 and large t1t_{1}. Alternatively, if the condition U/|t1|>9U/|t_{1}|>9 is satisfied together with not high off-site interactions, pressure is expected to work cooperatively to raise TcT_{\mathrm{c}}. Smaller V1/U,V2/U,…V_{1}/U,V_{2}/U,... and larger t1t_{1} could be prepared simultaneously by pressure as the present Hg1223 study demonstrated. Another possibility is to design a surface or interface with an insulating substrate that has a high dielectric constant to screen the off-site interaction.

VII Summary, Conclusions, and Outlook

We have elucidated why the triple-layer Hg1223 shows the highest TcT_{\mathrm{c}} as compared to the single-, double-, and infinite-layer cuprates at ambient pressure and a further increase in TcT_{\mathrm{c}} under pressure, together with the mechanism of SC. This has been achieved by examining the ground states of the ab initio low-energy effective Hamiltonians of Hg1223. To explore the pressure dependence of the superconductivity, we have investigated the systems under pressure ranging from 00 GPa to 6060 GPa. By using the VMC method, we have calculated the dd-wave SC order parameter FSCF_{\rm SC} in the thermodynamic limit and estimated TcT_{\mathrm{c}} by following the formula (26) and have found the stable and uniform dd-wave SC phase in the ground state in the hole concentration region 0.1<δ<0.250.1<\delta<0.25.

Hg1223 at ambient pressure is found to be in a slightly strong coupling region above the optimal value of U/|t1|∼9U/|t_{1}|\sim 9, which is the primary reason for high TcT_{\mathrm{c}} in comparison to single-, double-, and infinite-layer compounds studied in Ref. [72], where a high U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| value (because of large UU) originates from poorer screening. The pressure drives it into the weak coupling region over the optimum U/|t1|U/|t_{1}|, which contributes to keeping FSCF_{\rm SC} in the plateau region around the peak at weak pressure P<30P<30 GPa, while it works to sharply decrease FSCF_{\rm SC} at P>30P>30 GPa. However, it is partially compensated by the largely decreasing off-site interaction, which works to enhance FSCF_{\rm SC}. Then this interplay eventually makes a broad peak structure in the pressure dependence of FSCF_{\rm SC}.

As for TcT_{\mathrm{c}}, the pressure makes the increase in |t1||t_{1}|, which contributes to enhancing TcT_{\mathrm{c}}. In addition, the pressure makes a reduction of U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| as well, contributing to weak enhancement of TcT_{\mathrm{c}} cooperatively in the region of U/|t1|>9U/|t_{1}|>9 at low pressures <30<30 GPa. On the other hand, higher pressure above 3030 GPa corresponding to decreasing U/|t1|U/|t_{1}| below 8 causes a substantial reduction of TcT_{\mathrm{c}} due to the decay in FSCF_{\rm SC}, which becomes the dominant factor that controls TcT_{\mathrm{c}}. This interplay is perfectly consistent with the experimental dome structure. It demonstrates that one effective route to enhance the superconductivity is to reduce the off-site interaction within the moderate and not too weak range to avoid the stripe phases. The determination of the boundary between the SC and stripe phases requires careful analysis in the case of weaker off-site interaction and will be left for a subject of future work.

The TcT_{\mathrm{c}} formula at the optimal carrier density, Tc∼0.16​|t1|​FSCT_{\mathrm{c}}\sim 0.16|t_{1}|F_{\rm SC} established in the single-, double-, and infinite-layer cuprates 72 is shown to hold also in the triple-layer cuprates and to reproduce the essential feature of the pressure dependence, namely, the peak around 3030 GPa.

We have also found the tendency that, in the underdoped region (δ≲0.1\delta\lesssim 0.1), the filling in the IP is much closer to half filling than that in the OP. This stabilizes the AF order in the IP simultaneously retaining a weak SC order as the proximity from the OP SC and enables the coexistence of the SC and AF.

The effective instantaneous attraction for Hg1223 that induces the Cooper pair is found and its origin is identified as the mechanism of “attraction by reduced repulsion” emerging in the originally strongly repulsive onsite interaction term, which is common to the single-, double-, and infinite-layer cuprates. This mechanism is very general as is observed also in the SC phase of the Hubbard model. The Cooper pair formed by the instantaneous attraction is in contrast with the weak-coupling BCS SC caused by the retarded interaction with a large coherence length. The SC at the optimum doping of the cuprates does not belong to the BEC regime either, because the attraction is relatively weaker than the kinetic energy scale (namely, effective Fermi energy expected from a large Fermi surface) and the preformed pair is not well developed above TcT_{\mathrm{c}}. In fact, FSCF_{\rm SC} and TcT_{\mathrm{c}} at the optimum doping rather increase with the increased attraction in the realistic cuprates as Eq. (28) suggests, instead of the reduction expected in the typical BEC regime.

In the underdoped region toward the Mott insulator, Eq. (26) shares similarity with the BKT transition of a weakly interacting 2D Bose gas in the proportionality of TcT_{\mathrm{c}} to the superfluid density FSCF_{\rm SC}, which is interpreted as the “boson density”. However, Eq. (28) indicates that the “boson density” is controlled in a nontrivial fashion by the emergent attractive interaction and the hole density in the present case. Despite the high electron density in the underdoped region, at which one can naively expect a large Fermi surface in metals, the cuprates do not show a diverging electron effective mass by keeping the high density of coherent electrons as a route to the Mott insulator. Instead, the incoherent part becomes dominating toward the Mott insulator, and the effective “boson” emerges as Eq. (28), if one can ignore the randomness and inhomogeneity in real materials.

A stringent test of the emergence of instantaneous attraction is to experimentally measure Eq. (31), for instance, by neutron scattering. Energy-momentum-resolved data will unveil the dynamical origin of the attraction.

The emergent attraction may cause the fractionalization of electrons 72; 36, which is now supported by various experimental and theoretical studies 67; 66; 36; 37; 83; 73; 69. To reach a further complete understanding of the superconductivity, it is desired to uncover the nature of the fractionalized hidden fermion splintered from the original electron and examine whether the weakly bound exciton proposed in the literature 68; 36 is involved in the fractionalization.

There exist other strong-coupling unconventional SCs such as the iron-based SCs 41 and nickel oxide SCs 47; 75. It is an intriguing future subject to clarify whether these families have the common aspect to the cuprates along the line we reported in this paper. The relations to heavy-electron SC in ff-electron systems and 4dd-electron SC are also intriguing in a more general perspective of the fractionalization. Applying the present framework to other trilayer cuprates, such as Bi2223 14 and compounds containing even more layers, would also be intriguing to examine the broader applicability of the proposed SC mechanism, which is left for future studies. Although their experimentally observed TcT_{\mathrm{c}} values are lower and their treatment is beyond the scope of the present work because of the higher computational cost, multilayer compounds with four or more layers would also be interesting future targets.

In terms of the materials design strategy for higher TcT_{\mathrm{c}}, one can propose to seek materials that allow “attraction by reduced repulsion” from the “false vacuum”, as well as tuning toward optimum onsite repulsion, weaker intersite interaction, and larger bandwidth. Our findings will stimulate research on designing and optimizing SCs toward a higher SC critical temperature by explicitly utilizing the mechanism of the emergence of the attraction from the repulsion.
